Memory

How to choose RAM for your gaming PC

Understand RAM capacity, DDR compatibility, memory kits and speed profiles so you can choose a sensible upgrade.

By PC Part Performance · September 18, 2026
On this pageChoose compatibility before speedWork out how much capacity you needBuy a kit and use the recommended slotsRead the speed rating in contextCheck the upgrade before keeping itWatch the walkthroughSources
The short answer

Match the DDR generation and supported kit to your platform, then choose capacity around your real workload. Extra capacity and a faster memory profile solve different problems.

Choose compatibility before speed

Begin with the motherboard’s supported memory type and the processor’s memory specifications. Desktop DIMMs and laptop SODIMMs are different physical formats, and DDR generations are not interchangeable. A faster kit from the wrong generation will not solve a compatibility problem.

Use the exact motherboard support page to check capacity limits and tested kits. A kit not appearing on a compatibility list is not automatically incompatible, but a listed kit provides a more useful starting point than a similar-looking product name.

Source: Kingston: gaming memory support and kit compatibility

Work out how much capacity you need

Start with the recommended requirements of the games and applications you actually use. Then consider what runs alongside them: a browser, voice chat, recording software and large mods all compete for memory. There is no single capacity that guarantees smooth performance in every game.

On an existing PC, observe memory use during your normal workload rather than at idle. If the machine slows down while memory is heavily used, extra capacity may help. If there is already comfortable room, buying more memory alone is unlikely to transform your frame rate. Treat capacity and speed as different decisions.

Buy a kit and use the recommended slots

For a new build, choose one kit containing the capacity and number of modules you intend to use. Separately sold kits with matching labels are not guaranteed to work together at their advertised settings. Kingston specifically warns that mixing overclockable memory kits is unsupported.

Install the modules in the positions specified in the motherboard manual. Do not assume the first two adjacent slots are correct. Keep the remaining slots in mind for upgrades, but remember that adding modules can change the speeds a system can run reliably.

Source: Kingston: gaming memory support and kit compatibility

Read the speed rating in context

Memory transfer rate is commonly shown in MT/s. Latency timings describe another part of how memory behaves; neither number alone is a complete performance score. Compare game benchmarks on a similar platform before paying substantially more for a faster kit.

Advertised XMP or EXPO settings may require enabling a profile in firmware. These are overclocking profiles, and the achievable result depends on the processor, board, firmware and module configuration. Start with the motherboard instructions and check stability after changing settings.

Source: Intel: memory speed and processor limits

Check the upgrade before keeping it

After installation, confirm that the system detects the intended capacity. Check the operating speed, run a memory stability test, and use your regular games and applications. Crashes or memory errors are a reason to revisit settings or installation, not something to ignore.

Keep a simple record of the kit model, occupied slots and selected profile. It makes future troubleshooting easier and helps prevent an accidental mismatch when the next upgrade comes around.
